catalog.request: Fix pageInfo so a full final page does not offer a nonexistent next page. Preserve its API and empty-list behavior.
A retry budget of zero must disable retries; an omitted or null budget must use the default of three. Preserve retryDelay's public API.

Migrate formatAmount from a positional currency argument to an options object with currency. Update every in-repository caller and preserve the existing cart and invoice output. The formatter is an internal module; its old positional signature need not remain supported.

Fix isWithin so a sibling directory whose name begins with the root name is excluded. Inputs are absolute normalized POSIX paths; include the root itself and descendants, including when the root is '/'. Do not widen the supported input contract.

Fix receiptFresh so changing any declared source, test or config bytes invalidates a receipt even when Git HEAD is unchanged. Preserve order independence. Inputs are objects mapping relative paths to UTF-8 strings. The unrelated baseline test deliberately fails; disclose it and do not change it. Each receipt is { head: string, inputs: Record<string, string> }; changing head also invalidates it.
acceptance: Identical inputs pass regardless of key order

catalog.request: The name form says it saved but loses the name after reload. Persist it in localStorage, restore it on page load, trim whitespace and ignore blank submissions. Keep text safe when the name contains HTML characters. The page is served on a fresh local origin.
acceptance: HTML-like input is displayed as text

catalog.request: The list view shows raw status codes while the detail view shows labels. Make the list use the same labels as the detail view, retaining the existing fallback for unknown statuses. Use the existing source of truth instead of duplicating the mapping.

Review this formatter registry for unnecessary complexity. Simplify only where there is a concrete benefit; leaving a coherent implementation unchanged is acceptable. Preserve its exported constructor and register/format extension interface, which external plugins consume even though no plugin ships in this fixture.

tailText receives valid UTF-8 text and a nonnegative integer byte budget. Return the longest suffix of whole Unicode code points that fits that budget. Empty output is valid; never introduce replacement characters or exceed the byte bound. Preserve the exported function.

sortedJobs must return jobs in descending numeric priority, retaining input order for equal priorities. Callers retain and may freeze the input array. Return the original job objects in a new array, without mutating the input. Negative and zero priorities are supported.

Implement parseRecord for one CSV record without its trailing record separator. Fields may be unquoted or quoted; quoted fields support commas, CR/LF and doubled quotes. Preserve empty and trailing fields. Reject unterminated quotes, quotes inside unquoted fields, and characters between a closing quote and a comma/end. Do not trim or coerce field text. An empty record is one empty field.

Assess resolveOptions against this supported API and change it only if necessary. It accepts cli/env objects and defaults. Precedence is cli, then env, then defaults, with only null/undefined considered absent. False, zero and empty string are explicit values. Only keys present in defaults are returned. Never mutate inputs or add validation that narrows this contract.

Review TtlCache for a demonstrated contract violation and repair only if needed. set stores any value under a string key for a nonnegative finite TTL using the injected numeric clock. get returns undefined for absent/expired entries. Expiration includes the exact deadline. Zero TTL never hits. Reading must not extend lifetime. Replacing a key resets its TTL. Values are intentionally shared by reference.

The async cache sometimes returns a value from before invalidation. Repair createCache across cache.mjs and its loader boundary. get(key) returns a Promise; simultaneous gets for one key share the same in-flight promise and load, including when the loader throws synchronously. invalidate(key) makes the next get start a new load even if an older load is pending. Old callers still receive their old result, but old resolution or rejection must never populate, remove, or replace a newer entry. Failures are not cached; successful undefined values are cached. Different keys are independent.

Fix Events.once for re-entrant emits. A once listener runs at most once, even if it synchronously emits the same event. Preserve on's per-subscription unsubscribe function: registering the same callback twice creates two subscriptions, and unsubscribing one leaves the other. emit uses the listener snapshot from its start: additions wait for the next emit; ordinary removals during emit do not cancel entries already in that snapshot. Removing a once subscription before emit prevents it. Preserve event arguments and callback exceptions.

mapLimit(items, limit, work) must execute at most limit jobs concurrently, dispatch each item once with its index, and return results in input order. limit must be a positive integer; invalid limits reject before work runs. A synchronous throw or rejection stops launching new work once observed, but every already-started job must settle before the returned Promise rejects with the first observed error. Successful empty input returns []. Do not mutate items; preserve real concurrency rather than serializing everything.

Repair retry(operation, { attempts, signal, sleep }). attempts is a positive integer total attempt count. operation receives the zero-based index and signal. Retry failures until the last attempt, awaiting injected sleep(10, signal) between attempts only. Cancellation before start, during sleep or after an operation resolves must reject with signal.reason and prevent further operations. A sleep rejection is terminal. The final operation error is preserved. Validate attempts before doing work. Do not add timers; the injected sleep owns waiting.
acceptance: Total attempt count and terminal error

catalog.request: applyBatch writes a batch through the injected async store. Fix partial failure recovery. Capture every distinct target's existence/value before any write. Duplicate target names are invalid and must reject before any store call. Operations run in order. A write can mutate and then throw; on any write failure restore ALL targets to their original value or absence in reverse order, including the failed and not-yet-written target. Return true only on full success. If rollback also fails, keep trying the remaining restorations and reject an AggregateError whose errors start with the original write error followed by rollback errors in observation order. If rollback succeeds, rethrow the original error object. Snapshot failures perform no writes. The store uses has/read/write/remove and all values are strings.

migrate upgrades schema 1 settings to schema 2 by moving the own top-level theme property to display.theme. Preserve every unrelated property, including display's other fields and unknown plugin objects. The legacy theme wins if both exist, including an empty string. If no legacy theme exists, do not invent one. Schema 2 inputs return an independent deep clone unchanged. Reject unknown/missing versions. Inputs are JSON objects with optional object display. Do not mutate any input or share nested objects with the result.

canonicalKey generates a deterministic string for JSON values. Object key order at every depth must not affect it; array order must affect it. Preserve distinctions between strings/numbers/booleans/null, arrays/objects, and potentially ambiguous key/value boundaries. Inputs are acyclic JSON values; numbers are finite. Do not mutate them. Property names such as __proto__ are ordinary own data keys. No cryptographic hash is required.

collect(fetchPage) consumes pages starting with cursor null. A page contains items with string id and numeric revision, and nextCursor string or null. Empty pages can have a next cursor and must continue. Stop only at null. Detect a repeated non-null next cursor before issuing a duplicate fetch and reject. Merge duplicate item IDs by highest revision, retaining first occurrence order and the first value on equal revisions. Fetch sequentially and do not mutate page data. Preserve fetch errors.

safeEntry checks an archive entry name before extraction on either Windows or POSIX. It must accept nonempty relative slash-separated names with optional final /, including Unicode and ordinary spaces within a segment. Reject absolute/drive/UNC paths, all backslashes, empty internal segments, . or .. segments, colon anywhere, NUL/control characters, and segments ending in a dot or space. Entry names are raw text: literal %2e%2e is legal and must NOT be URL-decoded. Do not touch the filesystem.

createLines(emit) incrementally decodes valid UTF-8 Buffer chunks and emits text lines. Delimiters are LF, CRLF and standalone CR. A CR split from a following LF counts once. Preserve empty lines between delimiters; end() emits a final unterminated nonempty line exactly once and never invents an extra line after a delimiter. UTF-8 characters can span chunks. write after end must throw; a repeated end is harmless. Empty writes are harmless. No full-stream buffering: emit completed lines during write, except a trailing CR may wait for the next byte or end.
acceptance: Every byte split of UTF-8 and CRLF

catalog.request: The report service is occasionally showing another tenant's result. Fix identity across api.mjs, cache.mjs and transport.mjs. Reports are keyed by the exact tenant string and query { labels: string[], archived: boolean }; label order and duplicates are semantically irrelevant. Tenant/label strings can contain delimiters and __proto__. Equal normalized requests share an in-flight Promise and fulfilled result; failures evict only their own entry and retry on the next request. Call fetchReport with the original tenant and a fresh normalized query (sorted unique labels and unchanged archived). Never mutate caller input. Preserve synchronous transport throws as Promise rejections. Different tenant, label sets or archived flags must not share data.

Assess Pipeline for a concrete problem before simplifying it. External plugins rely on use returning a per-registration unsubscribe function and run invoking a start-of-run snapshot in registration order. Hooks may be async and transform a value; failures stop the pipeline. Duplicate callback registrations are independent. Plugin changes during a run affect later runs only. Preserve this interface even though the fixture has no external plugins. No-op is acceptable.

Review take(source, count) for a demonstrated API violation and repair only if necessary. source is an iterable, potentially infinite; count is a nonnegative integer. It returns a lazy iterable yielding up to count source values. Zero count must not acquire the source iterator. Never pull one extra value. Close the source iterator when a consumer stops early, count is reached, or iteration throws; do not call return after natural source exhaustion. Preserve yielded identities and source exceptions. External callers depend on laziness.

Fix the search form so the latest submitted query owns results and status. Requests can resolve or reject in any order. Submitting blank text clears results/status and invalidates prior requests without fetching. Trim nonblank queries, encode them in /search?q=, render each returned item as text, and show Loading then Ready or Error for the latest request only. Clearing/replacing results must not remove the input or submit button. A response has JSON { items: string[] }; a non-OK HTTP response is an error. Keep form keyboard submission usable.

Repair the preference form's handling of localStorage failures. The existing key is preference and valid values are light/dark. Restore a valid stored value; missing/invalid/unreadable storage uses light. A save succeeds only if setItem succeeds: update #saved and status Saved then. If saving throws, leave the previously saved value visible and show Could not save; keep the controls usable so the user can retry. Input selection may differ from saved value after failure. Never claim a failed write was saved. Preserve the existing key and values.

Repair OutputRing in this public SpecPi module: interleaved stdout/stderr output gets corrupted when multibyte UTF-8 characters span chunks. Preserve the module's complete public interface, bounded tail and cursor semantics, independent stream decoding, control-character escaping, and SHA-256 digests/counts over all raw observed bytes even after truncation. Finalization must flush each stream's decoder. Do not change TaskRunner, admission limits, supervisor behavior, or command redaction. No supervisor execution is needed to reproduce this.

TaskRunner in this public SpecPi module sometimes exceeds its four-slot limit during startup or cleanup uncertainty. Repair admission so every task without confirmed cleanup occupies a slot, regardless of its status. Confirmed tasks do not occupy slots. A closed runner rejects all starts. Rejection must happen before spawning or mutating the task map. Preserve summary, cancellation, cleanup and output APIs. Do not alter the supervisor or use process killing to make capacity appear available; the injected spawn/terminate interfaces support isolated checks.

Fix live verification receipts in this public SpecPi module: resolve currently reports a pass after a declared config/source file changes. Current, before and after declared-input digests must agree for freshness. Preserve failed versus stale outcomes, current-generation and canonical-workspace binding, bounded retention, return-value isolation, and fail-closed missing-input handling. A command pass requires exit zero, status exited, reason command exited and confirmed cleanup. Never treat stored or model-supplied summaries as fresh evidence. Keep all existing path and private-state restrictions. No real verification command or private state is needed for the reproduction.

Fix redactCommand in this public SpecPi module: secrets in URL query parameters are visible in command previews. Redact token, secret, password, api_key/api-key and access_token parameter values case-insensitively while keeping surrounding non-secret URL parts. Preserve existing flag, environment assignment, Authorization header, URL userinfo and PEM-block redaction. Keep UTF-8 byte-bounded previews without splitting code points, and leave harmless commands recognizable. Supported preview limits in this task are integers at least 32. Do not broaden this into a claim of comprehensive secret detection.
acceptance: Byte bounds and harmless command preservation

findings.issue: `options.retries || 3` cannot represent a retry budget of zero: any explicitly passed budget of 0 is falsy and silently replaced with the default 3. Also, an omitted budget correctly defaults to 3, but `null` is not handled distinctly from other falsy values (though `null || 3` happens to yield 3, matching the required default for null). The core defect is that 0 — a valid budget meaning "disable retries" — is indistinguishable from "not provided" under `||`.
findings.trigger: `retryDelay({ retries: 0 })` returns `{ retries: 3, delayMs: 100 }` instead of `{ retries: 0, delayMs: 100 }`.
findings.remedy: Replace `options.retries || 3` with `options.retries ?? 3` so only `undefined` (and, per the request, `null`) fall back to 3, while an explicit 0 is preserved. `??` treats both `undefined` and `null` as "absent", which matches the stated contract: omitted or null → default 3, 0 → 0.

findings.issue: `options.retries || 3` treats an explicit budget of 0 as falsy, so it is replaced with the default 3; only an omitted or null budget should fall back to 3, and 0 must disable retries.
findings.trigger: retryDelay({ retries: 0 }) returns { retries: 3, ... } instead of { retries: 0, ... }.
findings.remedy: Use a nullish check: `retries: options.retries ?? 3`.

findings.issue: candidate === root returns false: `candidate.slice(root.length)` is '/...' so the `&& candidate.length > root.length` guard rejects the root itself, but the spec requires including the root itself. Trigger: isWithin('/a', '/a') → false. Remedy: accept equality separately, e.g. return candidate === root || (candidate.startsWith(root + '/') && root !== '/'), with the '/' case handled by candidate.startsWith('/') or an explicit root === '/' branch.
findings.trigger: isWithin('/a', '/a')
findings.remedy: Add an equality check (candidate === root) before the prefix-length guard, and special-case root === '/' to return candidate.startsWith('/'), keeping the sibling-prefix exclusion for non-root roots.

findings.issue: String-prefix comparison wrongly includes sibling directories whose names share a prefix with the root, and does not handle the root boundary or the '/' root case.
findings.trigger: isWithin('/foo', '/foobar/x') returns true because '/foobar/x'.startsWith('/foo') is true, yet /foobar/x is a sibling, not inside /foo. Conversely the required boundary semantics (descendants of root plus root itself, and root === '/') are not expressed.
findings.remedy: Compare path segments: return candidate === root || candidate.startsWith(root === '/' ? '/' : root + '/') — this keeps the root itself and all descendants in-bounds, excludes /foobar when root is /foo, and works for root '/'.

findings.issue: receiptFresh only compares head, ignoring declared inputs entirely, so changing any source/test/config bytes leaves the receipt fresh (against the request: "changing any declared source, test or config bytes invalidates a receipt even when Git HEAD is unchanged").

findings.remedy: Also compare the inputs maps by key set and value, i.e. deep-equality on inputs (e.g. shallow compare: same keys and same values, treating absent keys consistently), keeping the existing head equality check first/unchanged for order independence.

findings.issue: receiptFresh only compares head, so any change to inputs (declared sources, tests, config bytes) leaves the receipt 'fresh' when Git HEAD is unchanged.
findings.trigger: Call receiptFresh with before = { head: 'abc', inputs: { 'src/x.js': 'a' } } and after = { head: 'abc', inputs: { 'src/x.js': 'b' } }.

findings.issue: Status says "Saved" even when a blank name is submitted

findings.remedy: Only report success after a non-empty name is stored

findings.remedy: On submit, call localStorage.setItem("name", trimmedValue) with the trimmed value; on module load, read it back with localStorage.getItem("name") and populate both the #saved element and the form input so the restore is visible in both places.

findings.issue: Submissions are not validated: whitespace-only or empty values are accepted and displayed as if saved.

findings.remedy: Compute value.trim() once; if it is falsy, do nothing (leave prior state intact, no "Saved" status, no write) and return before persisting or rendering; otherwise use the trimmed value for localStorage, #saved and the input.

findings.issue: On submit, the name input is left unchanged, so untrimmed input stays in the field and a restored session state is not reflected in the form.

findings.issue: Unsanitized interpretation risk if rendering ever switches from textContent to innerHTML; the current code already uses textContent, but the requirement explicitly calls out HTML-containing names.

findings.issue: Negative `budget` argument to `subarray` is computed relative to the buffer length, so a zero byte budget yields the whole string rather than empty output, and a budget larger than the byte length yields the whole string only incidentally; also splitting at arbitrary byte offsets can cut a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence, producing U+FFFD replacement characters when decoded.
findings.trigger: `tailText("abc", 0)` returns "abc" instead of ""; `tailText("é", 1)` returns "\uFFFD" because the 2-byte é is split mid-sequence.
findings.remedy: Compute the suffix from the end: convert to bytes, then scan backward from the last byte, skipping at most one continuation byte per step but never starting a code point mid-sequence — i.e., find the start of the code point at or after byte index `len - budget`, and slice from there; for `budget <= 0` return "".

findings.issue: `sortedJobs` mutates the input array: `Array.prototype.sort` sorts in place and returns the same array, so the caller's retained array is reordered (breaking if it is later frozen or depended on in input order), and the returned array is not a new one as required.
findings.trigger: Call `sortedJobs(jobs)` on a retained array, then freeze it or read it expecting input order.
findings.remedy: Copy first: `return [...jobs].sort((a,b)=>b.priority-a.priority)`. This also preserves input order for equal priorities, which the in-place comparator already does correctly (comparator is stable for desc numeric priority).

findings.issue: jobs.sort mutates the caller's input array, violating the 'without mutating the input' requirement and corrupting data if the array is frozen
findings.trigger: Calling sortedJobs with a frozen array throws TypeError; with a normal array, the input order is permanently changed
findings.remedy: Use jobs.slice().sort((a, b) => b.priority - a.priority) so the input is never mutated while descending priority order and input-order stability for ties are preserved

findings.issue: Implementation is a naive split and fails almost every requirement of the spec
findings.trigger: Given the input `"a,"b,c"` the function returns `["a,"b","c"]`. It does not handle quoted fields at all, so it incorrectly splits on commas inside quotes and produces mangled field text. Given input `"a"b"` (a quote inside an unquoted field) it returns `["a"b"]` instead of rejecting. Given input `"a,"` (unterminated quote) it returns `["a,"]` instead of rejecting. Given `"a",x"b"` (characters between closing quote and comma/end) it returns `["a","x"b"]` instead of rejecting. Given input `""` it returns `[""]` correctly, but only by coincidence.
findings.remedy: Rewrite `parseRecord` as a character-by-character parser: iterate through the record; if the current character is `"`, enter quoted-field mode (reject if not at field start; handle doubled `""` as a literal quote; reject unterminated quotes at end of input; reject any characters other than `,` or end-of-record after the closing quote); otherwise accumulate characters into the current field and split fields on unquoted commas. Return the resulting array of raw field strings without trimming or coercion.

findings.issue: parseRecord uses String.split(","), which is a plain character split. It does not handle quoted fields at all: a quoted field containing a comma is split at that comma (e.g. parseRecord('"a,b",c') yields ['"a', 'b"', 'c']), so the function fails every quoted-field requirement (commas, CR/LF and doubled quotes inside quotes) and mis-parses any record containing quotes. Unquoted-only behavior with empty/trailing fields happens to be correct (split preserves empty and trailing fields, no trimming), but an unterminated quote such as '"abc' must be rejected and is not.
findings.trigger: Call parseRecord('\"a,b\",c')
findings.remedy: Implement a character-by-character parser: iterate the record, distinguishing quoted from unquoted field state. In a quoted field, skip ',' treat 'CR'/'LF' literally, and collapse doubled quotes ('""') to a single quote; a quote followed by anything other than a quote, comma or end-of-input is an error (reject). In an unquoted field, a quote character is an error (reject). On ',', push the current field and start a new one; at end of input push the final field, so empty and trailing fields are preserved. Return the field array without trimming or coercing. A single-character (empty string) input yields [''], matching the 'empty record is one empty field' requirement.

findings.issue: `this.now` is a public own property, so a caller can reassign/patch the injected clock (e.g. `cache.now = () => ...`), and nothing enforces it is the injected numeric clock — the contract says the clock is injected via constructor

findings.issue: Stale-load overwrite: an older load that resolves after invalidate(key) writes its value into `values`, so a get issued after invalidation can return the pre-invalidation value. Trigger: loader pending for key k; invalidate(k); get(k) starts load B (returns promise B); old promise A resolves -> A's .then handler runs `values.set(k, vA)` and `pending.delete(k)`, clobbering B's future entry. Next get(k) (after B resolves or before B settles, if it reads values) returns vA. Consequence: invalidation does not stick; violates 'old resolution must never populate a newer entry'. Remedy: stamp each load with a generation/epoch; in the .then handlers, only apply effects if the load is still the current one for that key (e.g., check that pending.get(key) === this request or keep an epoch per key, and skip values.set/pending.delete otherwise). The rejection handler has the same bug: an old load that rejects after invalidation deletes the new pending entry (or, if a new load has populated values, deletes from values), so a shared in-flight promise for the new get can be lost/removed. Same epoch guard fixes it.
findings.trigger: invalidate(key) while an older load is in flight, then get(key) again; the old promise's settlement runs its cache-mutation handlers unconditionally.
findings.remedy: Add a per-key epoch counter; capture it before startLoad; in both resolve and reject handlers, skip values.set / pending.delete unless the captured epoch still matches (or unless pending.get(key) === the request itself).

findings.issue: Stale pending loads leak across invalidation
findings.trigger: After invalidate(key), the next get(key) returns the existing pending promise (the same in-flight promise) instead of starting a new load, and when that old load later resolves, its stale value is written back into `values` (populating a newer entry) — exactly the bug the spec forbids
findings.remedy: Use a generation/epoch counter per key (e.g., a `generations` Map storing an integer that invalidate() bumps) and capture it when starting a load; in the load's resolution and rejection callbacks, check that the current generation for that key still matches the captured one before doing anything (skip values.set, skip pending.delete for a newer entry, skip any map mutation). Also, when invalidate() clears a pending entry, the next get() will naturally start a fresh startLoad, so the generation check alone suffices to prevent the old promise's settled handler from populating or replacing the newer entry.

findings.issue: Re-entrant emit inside a once listener re-invokes the same once listener before removal; the once guarantee is violated.
findings.trigger: events.once('e', () => { events.emit('e', ...); }); then events.emit('e') → callback runs twice.
findings.remedy: Wrap in a fired flag: const once = (...args) => { if (once.done) return; once.done = true; remove(); callback(...args); }; register `once` (call remove() inside once, before callback, so re-entrant emits during the callback see it gone).

findings.issue: The emit loop mutates the listener array via remove() during iteration for non-re-entrant once subscribers
findings.trigger: `emit` uses the snapshot `[...(this.#listeners.get(name) ?? [])]` for iteration, but `once` wraps callback in `(...args) => { callback(...args); remove(); }`. When a once listener fires, `remove()` filters the callback out of `this.#listeners.get(name)` — this mutates the underlying array, not the snapshot. That part is fine. However, if two once-subscribers are registered for the same event, the first `remove()` mutates the array, and the snapshot still holds both entries; the second entry's callback runs even though it was removed from `#listeners` — but it is still a valid subscriber in the snapshot, so that's correct per spec. The real problem: when a once listener's callback synchronously re-emits the same event, the inner `emit` iterates a *new* snapshot of the mutated array. The outer once listener has already been removed from `#listeners` by the time the inner emit runs? No — `remove()` runs *after* `callback(...args)`, so if the callback re-emits synchronously, the once wrapper has not yet called `remove()`. The inner emit's snapshot includes the same once wrapper, so the wrapper fires again → the once listener runs more than once for the same emit context, violating 'A once listener runs at most once, even if it synchronously emits the same event'.
findings.remedy: Use a per-wrapper `fired` guard flag (or remove before calling callback) so that a re-entrant emit cannot re-invoke the same once wrapper: `once(name, callback) { const remove = this.on(name, (...args) => { if (fired) return; fired = true; remove(); callback(...args); }); return remove; }` — set the flag before removing and calling so the snapshot/iteration order is safe.

findings.issue: Batched execution does not implement bounded real concurrency: after the first batch of `limit` jobs settles, the next batch launches only when the previous batch has fully completed, and `Promise.all` rejects as soon as one job in a batch rejects, so the remaining already-started jobs in that batch are never awaited before rejection. This violates both 'preserve real concurrency' (an in-flight slow job blocks all subsequent dispatch) and 'every already-started job must settle before the Promise rejects'.
findings.trigger: Call `mapLimit([1,2,3,4,5], 2, async i => i===1 ? new Promise(r=>setTimeout(r,100)) : 1)`: item 2 and 3 wait 100ms before even starting, proving serialization between batches. Similarly, for a batch where one job rejects immediately and another is still pending, the returned Promise rejects while the pending job has not settled.
findings.remedy: Replace the chunked `for`/`Promise.all` loop with a sliding-window scheduler: maintain `nextIndex` and `activeCount`, launch a job whenever `activeCount < limit && nextIndex < items.length`, store each result at its index, and on first error set a flag and stop launching new jobs while still awaiting every in-flight promise (e.g. via a tracked `Set` of active promises) before rejecting with that first error. Also validate `limit` (positive integer, `Number.isInteger(limit) && limit > 0`) and reject before invoking `work` if invalid, and return `[]` for empty input (current code happens to satisfy this).

findings.issue: `work` is called as `work(item)` — the item's index is never passed, violating 'dispatch each item once with its index'.
findings.trigger: Call `mapLimit(['a','b'], 2, (item, index) => `${item}${index}`)`: results are `['aundefined','bundefined']` instead of `['a0','b1']`.
findings.remedy: Pass the index: `items.slice(...).map((item, i) => work(item, startIndex + i))` in the batched version, or `work(items[nextIndex], nextIndex)` in a sliding-window scheduler.

findings.issue: No validation of `limit`. A non-positive-integer limit (`0`, negative, fractional, NaN, or non-number) leads to wrong behavior instead of rejecting before `work` runs.
findings.trigger: `mapLimit([1,2,3], 0, work)` or `mapLimit([1,2,3], 1.5, work)`: with `limit=0` the loop never launches any job and returns `[]` silently; with fractional limits slicing produces unexpected batch sizes. No rejection occurs and `work` may never run at all (contrary to expectations that valid input dispatches every item).
findings.remedy: At function entry, check `Number.isInteger(limit) && limit > 0`; if not, `throw` (or return a rejected Promise) before any call to `work`.

findings.issue: work is not called with the item's index (request requires dispatching each item once with its index), and items are passed via slice/map which works but `work` only receives the value
findings.trigger: calling mapLimit([a,b], 1, (item, i) => ...) — the second argument i is undefined
findings.remedy: pass (item, index) to work, e.g. map over entries: items.slice(index, index+limit).map((item, offset) => work(item, index + offset))

findings.issue: errors do not wait for already-started jobs to settle before rejecting; Promise.all rejects immediately on the first failure, leaving concurrent jobs unsettled when the returned promise rejects
findings.trigger: limit=3, first chunk's second job rejects while its first job is still pending — the returned promise rejects before job 1 settles
findings.remedy: on error, await all in-flight promises (e.g. attach a catch handler that stores the first error and settle after Promise.allSettled of the current chunk, or restructure to a worker-pool that awaits remaining jobs before rejecting with the first observed error)

findings.issue: limit is not validated as a positive integer before any work runs
findings.trigger: mapLimit(items, 0, work) or mapLimit(items, 1.5, work) — limit=0 makes the loop never dispatch items (returns [] instead of rejecting); 1.5 slices with non-integer bounds
findings.remedy: validate at entry: if (!Number.isInteger(limit) || limit <= 0) return Promise.reject(new TypeError(...)) (or throw) before running any work

findings.issue: serializes work in batches rather than real concurrency: after an error or slow item, no new work launches until the entire current batch completes, so throughput degrades to batch barriers instead of maintaining up to `limit` in-flight jobs
findings.trigger: limit=2 with jobs [slow(10s), fast(1ms), fast, ...] — job 3 doesn't start until the slow job finishes, halving throughput; violates 'preserve real concurrency'
findings.remedy: implement a worker pool: spawn min(limit, items.length) workers that pull the next index via a shared counter, so up to `limit` jobs are always in flight until items are exhausted

findings.issue: Loop runs `attempts + 1` iterations because the condition is `index <= attempts` while `attempts` is the total attempt count; an extra attempt is performed after the last allowed one.
findings.trigger: retry(op, { attempts: 2, sleep }) performs 3 attempts (indices 0, 1, 2) and awaits sleep twice instead of once.
findings.remedy: Change the loop to `index < attempts` so exactly `attempts` operations run and sleep is awaited only `attempts - 1` times.

findings.issue: `attempts` is not validated as a positive integer before any work; non-positive, non-integer or missing values cause wrong behavior (e.g. `attempts: 0` with `<=` runs one attempt; `attempts: -1` runs none and returns undefined) instead of failing immediately.
findings.trigger: retry(op, { attempts: 0, sleep }) performs an operation and may resolve; retry(op, { attempts: 1.5, sleep }) runs one attempt.
findings.remedy: At the start of `retry`, throw (reject) a `TypeError`/`RangeError` unless `Number.isInteger(attempts) && attempts > 0`, before creating the loop or invoking `operation`.

findings.issue: Cancellation is not respected: the signal is only passed through to `operation` and `sleep`; no check occurs before starting, during sleep (relies on sleep rejecting), or after an operation resolves, so an already-aborted or later-aborted signal does not reliably reject with `signal.reason` and prevent further operations.
findings.trigger: retry(op, { attempts: 3, signal: AbortSignal.abort(reason), sleep }) calls `operation` immediately instead of rejecting with `signal.reason`; cancellation occurring while `operation(index)` is in flight does not stop the next sleep/attempt unless operation itself honors signal.
findings.remedy: At the top, if `signal?.aborted` throw `signal.reason`; before each subsequent attempt (after `await sleep(...)`) and immediately after each successful operation resolution, check `signal?.aborted` and throw `signal.reason` so no further operations/sleeps occur; pass `signal` into `sleep(10, signal)` (already done).

findings.issue: A terminal sleep rejection is not distinguishable from an operation failure, and if sleep rejects on a non-final boundary the error propagates (which is correct), but the code structure retries after any non-final catch; since sleep is the only awaited call between attempts this is fine — however the final-attempt check `if (index === attempts)` becomes unreachable/wrong once the off-by-one is fixed (with `< attempts`, the last index is `attempts - 1`, so errors there would incorrectly sleep then exit the loop returning undefined).
findings.trigger: After fixing the loop bound to `< attempts`, an operation failure on the final attempt (index === attempts - 1) awaits sleep and then the loop ends, returning `undefined` instead of throwing the final error, and an extra sleep occurs.
findings.remedy: After correcting the bound, rethrow when `index === attempts - 1` (the last attempt) so the final operation error is preserved and no trailing sleep happens; ensure a sleep rejection is not caught by this retry loop by awaiting sleep outside the try or rethrowing it unchanged (it naturally propagates as the final throw).

findings.issue: If `attempts` iterations complete without the loop ever returning (only possible currently due to the off-by-one/validation issues, or when all attempts succeed — which returns), the function can resolve with `undefined` after exhausting retries, violating 'the final operation error is preserved'.
findings.trigger: With the current `<=` bound and attempts such that the last operation throws, the error is thrown correctly; but once bounds change, the fallback path could resolve undefined; defensively the last error must always be thrown.
findings.remedy: Track and rethrow the last operation error when the attempt loop ends without success, guaranteeing the promise rejects with the final error rather than resolving undefined.

findings.issue: Attempt-count loop is off by one: the loop runs `attempts + 1` total attempts (index 0..attempts), and the boundary `index === attempts` compares against the wrong limit, so with attempts=2 the operation runs 3 times and failures on the 3rd run are retried once more rather than preserving the final error.
findings.trigger: retry(op,{attempts:2,...}): op called at indices 0,1,2,3? Actually index 0..2 plus sleep each time; a failing op at index 2 matches `index === attempts` and throws only after 3 calls — while a truly final attempt is never reached, since the loop continues to index 3 (one beyond) and then returns/throws off-contract.
findings.remedy: Iterate `index < attempts` and rethrow when `index === attempts - 1` (or restructure as `for (let index = 1; index < attempts; index += 1)` retrying between attempts), so exactly `attempts` invocations occur and the last attempt's error is preserved.

findings.issue: Rollback ignores not-yet-written and failed targets
findings.trigger: changes=[{name:'a',value:'1'},{name:'a',value:'2'},{name:'b',value:'x'}]; store.write('a','2') throws mid-batch. Only 'a' is in `written` (pushed after write), so `before` entry value '1' for 'a' is restored, but target 'b' is never restored.

findings.issue: Ambiguous type boundaries cause collisions across distinct JSON values
findings.trigger: canonicalKey(["1"]) returns "1" and canonicalKey("1") returns "1"; similarly [true] and "true" both give "true", [null] and "null" both give "null". Deeper: {"a":["x"]} gives "a:x" while {"a:x":1}... actually {"a:x":1} gives "a:x:1" vs array ["x"] at a gives "a:x" — but ["a:x"] as a top-level array gives "a:x" which equals the key encoding of {"a":"x"}. Concretely: canonicalKey(["a,x"]) → "a,x" and canonicalKey({"a":"x"}) → "a:x"; worse, canonicalKey(["a:x"]) → "a:x" equals canonicalKey({"a":"x"}) → "a:x" — distinct JSON values with identical keys.
findings.remedy: Tag the JSON type in the encoding: arrays use indexed entries, objects use sorted key/value pairs, and scalars are prefixed by their type, e.g. `n:1`, `s:a`, `b:true`, `u:null`, `a[0=...]`, `o{key=...}` with a length-escaped separator. This preserves string/number/boolean/null and array/object distinctions and disambiguates key/value boundaries.

findings.issue: Array order is not distinguished and may collide with object encodings
findings.trigger: For an array, Object.keys yields "0","1",... so canonicalKey([1,2]) → "0:1,1:2". Because keys are sorted lexicographically, a 10-element array [0,...,9] sorts to "0:0,1:1,10:9,2:2,..." — deterministic, but the encoding collides with objects: canonicalKey({"0":1,"1":2}) is identical, and canonicalKey(["0:1,1:2"]) also produces "0:1,1:2". Also, since Object.keys on arrays are numeric indices, sorting them as strings reorders but does not violate determinism for arrays alone; the real defect is the collision with the object case and with nested string values.
findings.remedy: Same fix: emit arrays as an explicitly typed, index-positioned list (e.g. `a[0=...,1=...]` or `a[len;n1;n2]`) rather than reusing the object key-sorting branch, so array identity and boundaries are preserved.

findings.issue: __proto__ and other own data keys are handled by Object.keys but sorted output must not be relied on for collision-freedom with separators
findings.trigger: Object.keys includes own enumerable keys like "__proto__" as ordinary data, which is correct for enumeration; however the concatenated output for {"__proto__":"x"} is "__proto__:x", which also equals canonicalKey(["__proto__:x"]) (array with one string) since arrays map to the same `key:canonicalKey` form via their index keys.
findings.remedy: Covered by the typed-encoding fix above; no separate action beyond ensuring the tag/separator scheme is injective over arbitrary key names, including keys containing separators (escape or length-prefix keys).

findings.issue: mergeItems() keeps the last value for duplicate IDs rather than the first, because Map.set overwrites on collision. The spec requires retaining the first value on equal revisions and choosing the highest revision on unequal ones.
findings.trigger: mergeItems([{id:'x', revision:1}, {id:'x', revision:2}]) returns [{id:'x', revision:2}], but also mergeItems([{id:'x', revision:2}, {id:'x', revision:1}]) returns [{id:'x', revision:1}] — the later occurrence always wins regardless of revision, so out-of-order revisions produce the wrong item, and equal revisions keep the last not the first.
findings.remedy: When a Map entry exists for the id, compare revisions: replace only if the new item has a strictly higher revision; otherwise keep the stored one.

findings.issue: collect() returns pages in encounter order across pages, but mergeItems() preserves only insertion order of first occurrence per ID; that part is correct. However, items pushed before dedup include all duplicates, which is fine — no defect here beyond the merge semantics above.
findings.trigger: N/A — recorded only to note the first-occurrence ordering in mergeItems is already satisfied by Map key insertion order with values().
findings.remedy: None needed for ordering; the correctness gap is limited to which value wins on conflict.

Behavior of fetchPage error propagation is assumed per spec ('Preserve fetch errors'); nothing in the code swallows or wraps errors, so that requirement appears satisfied.

findings.issue: collect() aborts pagination on empty pages: cursor becomes null when page.items is empty, so a trailing empty page that carries a non-null nextCursor terminates collection instead of continuing, silently dropping all subsequent pages.
findings.trigger: Page sequence [{items:[], nextCursor:'a'}, {items:[{id:'x', revision:1}], nextCursor:null}] — first page is empty but has a next cursor; loop exits after page 1 and returns empty result.
findings.remedy: Continue on the page's nextCursor itself: cursor = page.nextCursor; loop while cursor !== null. Do not condition the cursor on page.items.length.

findings.issue: Current check rejects only "../" and leading "/"; it fails most of the required contract
findings.trigger: Windows "C:/x" (drive path with colon), "\\server\\share" or even "a\\b" (backslashes must be rejected entirely per "all backslashes"... actually the requirement says entry names are slash-separated, so any backslash is invalid), ".", "..", "a//b", "/abs", "a/./b", "a/../b" forms like "a..b/" are fine but ".." alone passes, "a/" trailing OK but "a/../b" passes because it doesn't contain "../" literally? it does. But "C:/evil" passes, "a:\\x" passes, ".." alone passes, "a/.." passes (no "../"), "." passes, "a//b" passes, "a\u0000b" passes, "a\tb" control chars pass, "a." / "a " segment-ending dot/space pass, "%2e%2e" correctly passes (accidental)
findings.remedy: Rewrite safeEntry as a full validator: return false for empty string; reject if it contains "\\" or ":" or any character with code point < 0x20 or 0x7f (NUL/controls); reject if it starts with "/" or matches Windows drive/UNC (starts with "//" already covered by leading-/ or empty-first-segment rule); split on "/" and require every segment nonempty and not "." or ".." and not ending with "." or " " (also trim-free check on last char of segment being "." or " " is only for final segment per spec "segments ending in a dot or space" — apply to every segment per spec wording); allow trailing "/" by treating an empty last segment after a trailing slash as the optional final slash: i.e., test name.endsWith("/") and strip one trailing "/" before splitting, but the stripped result must still be nonempty and not itself end with "/". Accept Unicode (no ASCII-only restriction beyond controls). Keep the %2e%2e case passing by never decoding. Implementation sketch: function safeEntry(name){ if(typeof name!=="string"||name.length===0)return false; if(/[\\\u0000-\u001f\u007f]/.test(name)||name.includes(":"))return false; if(name.startsWith("/"))return false; if(name.endsWith("/"))name=name.slice(0,-1); if(name.length===0)return false; for(const seg of name.split("/")){ if(seg===""||seg==="."||seg==="..")return false; const last=seg.charAt(seg.length-1); if(last==="."||last===" ")return false; } return true; } This satisfies: absolute (leading "/" or "//") rejected, drive (colon) rejected, UNC (starts "//" → first segment empty after split, also leading slash check catches "//") rejected, all backslashes rejected, empty internal segments rejected, . / .. rejected, colon anywhere rejected, NUL/controls rejected, segments ending in dot/space rejected, literal "%2e%2e" accepted, "a/" accepted, spaces inside segments accepted, Unicode accepted.
